items.title: Dative bond (coordinate covalent bond), printed as 3.13

source_refs.note: The topic printed as 3.13 (should be 3.1.3), printed pages 48-49 (Figure 3.3), with Quick Check 3.1 as the self-check.

blocks.title: Dative bond
blocks.text: A dative bond is formed between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms.

Let us consider the example of bond formation between H₂O and a proton (H⁺). H₂O has two covalent bonds and there are two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom. On the other hand, the proton is deficient in electrons. Therefore, the oxygen atom can donate its lone pair of electrons to the acceptor H⁺, and this results in the formation of a dative bond as in the following diagram (Figure 3.3(a)).

Carbon monoxide also contains a dative bond between oxygen and carbon atoms. Oxygen shares its two valence shell electrons with the carbon atom to make a normal double covalent bond. However, the valency of carbon is not satisfied with these bonds. It needs one more pair of electrons to complete its octet. Oxygen atom donates one of its lone pairs for the formation of a covalent bond, which is a dative bond as exhibited in Figure 3.3(b).

blocks.alt: Three examples of dative bond formation. (a) Water and H+; a blue curved arrow takes an oxygen lone pair to H+, and the product shows a red arrow from O to the new H. (b) CO: the 'Lewis structure' with three shared pairs, and the bond form with two lines and a red arrow from O to C. (c) O=O plus an oxygen free radical, labelled 'oxygen free radical'; a blue curved arrow shows a lone pair donated, giving ozone with O+ in the centre and an arrow to O-.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.3: Dative bond formation (a) oxonium (hydronium) ion, (b) carbon monoxide, (c) ozone molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.3; the printed caption swaps (b) and (c)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption swaps the panels, naming (b) ozone and (c) carbon monoxide; the figure and the text show carbon monoxide in (b) and ozone in (c), as captioned above.

The structure of ozone molecule is presented in Figure 3.3(c). It is formed by a reaction between the oxygen molecule with an oxygen atom (a free radical (O)). One of the oxygen atoms in the molecule donates a pair of electrons to make a coordinate covalent bond with this free radical. Therefore, the central atom has total three bonds including a double covalent bond on one side and a coordinate covalent bond on the other. It carries a positive charge, while the oxygen atom that accepts the lone pair carries a negative charge.

blocks.text:
a) Draw the Lewis structures of N₂ and CS₂ molecules?
b) How many electrons are there in the valence shell of B in BF₃? Does it have the ability to accept a lone pair of electrons?
c) Show the formation of a dative bond between NH₃ and BF₃.
